passage:
The rejection email arrived while Joseph was sitting in the college career cell, waiting for his appointment. "We regret to inform you..." He shut the laptop.
When the advisor, Ms Reena, called him in, he said breezily, "Oh, the exchange scholarship? Didn't get it. Honestly, I never really wanted it. That programme's overrated anyway. Cold city, too much theory."
Ms Reena glanced at his file. "You rewrote your essay four times."
Joseph shrugged. "Just practice."
"Okay," she said. "Would you like to request the panel's feedback? If you apply for anything else, it'll help."
He paused, then nodded, not quite meeting her eyes.

qa.q: How many times had Joseph rewritten his essay?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why does Joseph say he never really wanted the scholarship?
qa.a: Saying he didn't want it takes the sting out of the rejection, even though four rewrites show how much he cared.

qa.q: What did Ms Reena suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Requesting the panel's feedback, which turns the rejection into something Joseph can learn from instead of hiding behind 'overrated'.

qa.q: How might Ms Reena read Joseph's breezy tone?
qa.a: Ms Reena seems to see through it, having noticed the four rewrites, but chooses not to argue and offers a practical step instead.

grounding: A student turned down for an exchange scholarship tells the career advisor he never wanted it, though his rewritten essay says otherwise.

passage:
I'm Ganga, and Tushar has been my lab partner since first year. For three weeks this term he rewrote his essay for the semester-abroad scholarship every night, reading it aloud to me between titrations.
On Thursday the list came out. His name wasn't on it.
By lunch he was telling everyone at our canteen table, "Honestly, I never really wanted it. That programme's overrated. It's just a nice brochure and expensive rent." He laughed a lot while saying it.
I don't know what was going on inside him. Maybe he truly changed his mind. But I remember him showing me that brochure in October, pointing at the lab photos. And when the coordinator emailed an offer of feedback on the essays, he deleted it in front of me without opening it. "Why would I need that?" he said.

qa.q: How long did Tushar spend rewriting his scholarship essay?
qa.a: For three weeks this term he rewrote it every night.

qa.q: Why might calling the programme overrated feel reasonable to Tushar?
qa.a: Believing he never wanted it softens the sting of being left off the list; if the prize was worthless, losing it hurts less.

qa.q: What choice could have turned the rejection into something useful for Tushar?
qa.a: Opening the coordinator's feedback email instead of deleting it, since it could show what to improve before a future try.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Tushar's laughter at the canteen table?
qa.a: Ganga isn't sure what Tushar feels, but notices the laughter doesn't match the weeks of rewriting or the excitement over the lab photos, so it looks like it might be covering disappointment.

grounding: Shows, through a lab partner's eyes, a student turned down for a scholarship insisting he never wanted it, which eases the hurt but makes him throw away the feedback.

passage:
Day one. Jahnavi read the email twice on the bus: not selected for the music conservatory scholarship. By evening she was telling Rafiq on the phone, "It's fine. I never wanted to move to Chennai anyway. That place is overrated, all theory and no real music."
Day four. Rafiq forwarded a message from the conservatory offering short feedback calls to applicants. "Might be useful?" Jahnavi sent back a thumbs-up and didn't book one. Why bother, she thought, about a place I don't even care about. She practised her ragas and felt calmer than she had in weeks.
Day nineteen. The form for next year opened. Jahnavi sat with the laptop on her knees, the cursor blinking in a box that asked what she had worked on since. She realised she had no idea what the panel had heard in her audition. The feedback calls had closed last week.

qa.q: What did the conservatory offer applicants on day four?
qa.a: Short feedback calls to applicants.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi feel calmer after deciding the conservatory was overrated?
qa.a: If the place wasn't worth wanting, the rejection stopped stinging, so the disappointment eased and she could practise without the hurt.

qa.q: Which choice on day four cost Jahnavi later?
qa.a: Not booking a feedback call; she lost the chance to learn what the panel heard, which she needed once next year's form opened.

qa.q: What might Rafiq have been thinking when only a thumbs-up came back?
qa.a: Rafiq may have sensed Jahnavi was brushing off the disappointment and quietly worried that a useful chance would slip by.

grounding: Illustrates a student refused a scholarship deciding it was never wanted, which calms the disappointment but hides the lessons the attempt could have offered.

passage: In the office of the college scholarship cell in Nagpur, Suraj read the rejection letter twice, folded it, and turned to go. Professor Irawati, who ran the cell, caught him at the door. "Suraj, I'm sorry. Would you like feedback on your application?" "No need, ma'am. I never really wanted it. That exchange programme is overrated. Three months in a cold country, what's the use?" Professor Irawati nodded slowly. "You wrote four drafts of your essay." Suraj's jaw tightened. "That was just practice." "The panel had specific comments. They might help next year." "There won't be a next year. I'm not interested." He left. In the corridor, he took the letter out again and read the line "a strong candidate" three times. Then he put it away.

qa.a: Four drafts.

qa.q: Why did Suraj call the programme overrated?
qa.a: He felt deeply disappointed, and telling himself he never wanted it made the rejection hurt less.

qa.q: What could Suraj gain by accepting the feedback?
qa.a: He could learn what the panel thought, which might help next time, instead of hiding the chance to improve.

qa.q: How might Professor Irawati see Suraj's reaction?
qa.a: She likely sees the disappointment behind his words, since she knows he wrote four drafts, and hopes he'll come back for the feedback.

Before, 3 March: Madhuri spent four nights on the scholarship essay for the summer research programme in Bengaluru, reading it aloud to her roommate Binita. "If I get this, I'll finally feel like a real scientist."

During, 28 March: the email said no. Madhuri closed the laptop and announced, "Honestly, I never wanted it. It's glorified photocopying for professors. And Bengaluru in May? No thanks." Binita said, "You read that essay to me four times." Madhuri shrugged and put on a film.

After, 15 April: the programme sent feedback to every applicant. Madhuri didn't open it. When Binita asked, Madhuri said, "Why would I? It doesn't matter to me." But she scrolled past the email three times that week, and the next application form stayed empty on the desk.

qa.a: Madhuri spent four nights on the scholarship essay.

Sumit, you're sulking about the transfer, so let old Gurpreet tell you something. When I was twenty, in my second year at Ludhiana, I applied for a travel scholarship to study farm co-operatives in Denmark. I wrote the essay by lantern because of the power cuts. They turned me down.

That same evening I told my friends, "Good. Who wants to freeze in Denmark? Those programmes are for show." I said it so often I nearly believed it. A month later my professor, Dr Sandhu, called me in and asked, "Did you ask them why?" I hadn't. I was too busy pretending I never cared.

So I wrote to them. They said my plan for the visits was vague. Next year I applied again, clearer, and went. If I'd kept saying I never wanted it, I'd never have learned that.

qa.q: What did the scholarship committee say was wrong with the application?
qa.a: They said the plan for the visits was vague.

qa.q: Why did young Gurpreet keep saying the programmes were for show?
qa.a: Young Gurpreet felt disappointed and hurt by the rejection, and calling the programme worthless made the loss easier to carry.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Dr Sandhu's question "Did you ask them why?" led Gurpreet to write to the committee, learn what was vague, and succeed the next year.

qa.q: How might Dr Sandhu have seen young Gurpreet that month?
qa.a: Dr Sandhu probably noticed the brave talk covering disappointment, and chose one gentle question instead of a lecture.

grounding: An elder recalls dismissing a scholarship after being turned down, until asking why revealed what could be improved.

Chinmay read the rejection on a crawling local train, squeezed between a fish basket and the door, phone battery at four percent. "Not selected for the Tokyo exchange scholarship." Before the screen died, Aparna's message came through: "Any news?? 🤞"

He typed fast: "Didn't get it. Honestly relieved. Nobody learns anything on those exchanges, it's a holiday with a certificate." Then the phone went black.

For the rest of the ride he kept building the case: the food would be strange, the lab was probably average, he'd miss his cousin's wedding. By Dadar station it sounded almost convincing.

At home, charging the phone, he saw Aparna's reply: "You made me proofread that statement five times. Did they send any feedback?" He looked at the folder named "Tokyo final" and didn't open it. Not yet.

qa.q: How much battery did Chinmay's phone have on the train?
qa.a: Chinmay's phone battery was at four percent.

qa.q: Why did "Honestly relieved" feel true to Chinmay on the train?
qa.a: Chinmay was disappointed and embarrassed, and calling the exchange a holiday softened the sting in a crowded, tiring moment.

qa.q: What would you advise Chinmay to do with the "Tokyo final" folder?
qa.a: Open it with Aparna, read any feedback, and note what to change for the next application, rather than deciding it never mattered.

grounding: Shows a student, rejected for an exchange scholarship on a crowded train, deciding it was never worth wanting and leaving the lessons unopened.

passage: Two years ago I applied for the state merit scholarship and didn't get it. Within an hour I had decided I never wanted it anyway. I told my friend Yogesh the programme was for "bookworms", that the stipend was tiny, that I would have hated the rules. I said it so often I almost believed it. Yogesh just said, "Okay, Santosh," in a way that annoyed me. Months later, helping a junior apply, I read the selection criteria properly for the first time. Community work: I had none. Interview practice: I had skipped it. That hurt more than the rejection. The sour story had kept me from learning anything. This year I applied again, with both. I got an interview.

qa.q: What made Santosh feel more hurt than the rejection itself?

qa.q: What did Santosh do differently the second time?
qa.a: Built up community work and practised interviews before applying again, and got an interview.

qa.a: Probably sceptical but patient, saying "Okay, Santosh" rather than arguing.

Mentor's note, first week of the Onam break.
Ganga came by to return a book and mentioned, very brightly, that the exchange scholarship results were out and she hadn't got it. "Honestly, I never wanted it. That programme is overrated. Everyone just goes for the photos." Two months ago she rewrote her essay four times in this office.
Her friend Nirmala, waiting at the door, looked at the floor.
I didn't argue. I said it was fine to feel disappointed even about something overrated, and asked if she'd like to read the panel's feedback together after the break. She said, "Maybe," and left quickly.
Next step: I've kept Thursday at four free and emailed her the feedback, so it's there when she is ready.

qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why did Ganga say she never wanted the scholarship?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and embarrassed, and believing the programme was overrated eased the sting of being turned down.
